attributes.title: Level 3

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use comments to create multiple sections in the editor to better organize your code?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code might be placed underneath each comment?

❓ How do you create blank lines in the JavaScript editor?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that typing // tells the project to skip over the text that follows and move onto the next line of code. Just as when naming sprites, it’s useful to be short and descriptive when writing comments. 

💡 Point out to the ninja that they are welcome to use different images or variable names in this project. They can click the palette to change the image.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by adding code comments to organize where the code will go in the editor!


Notice there is already code in the editor; there are three blank image variables under the comment // sprite images. Select images for each variable, then update the variable name accordingly. 


Underneath this starter code, add comments with these descriptions to the project: array and variable set up, project code.


Start each comment with // and add several blank lines between each comment.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you declare a new array and type the image variable names inside the brackets [ ]?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How was an array created in the blocks editor? How is it similar and different to creating an array in the JavaScript editor?

❓ What keywords and symbols do you notice in the array declaration code?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that an array is an ordered list of elements with the same data type. An array can be made up of images, string, number, or sprite values. All elements in the array must be of the same type.

💡 In the blocks editor, the ninja used a [set list to] block to create a new array. If the ninja wanted to create an array of a different type, they would drag in either an image or text bubble. Similarly, in the JavaScript editor, specific symbols need to be used to indicate the array type. For images, the ninja should use img `..`. In this example, the images are stored as variables, and as such, the variable names can be typed directly into the array. 

💡 Arrays are declared in the same way as variables in JavaScript. However, the elements of an array must be contained by brackets [ ]. Point out to the ninja that like other symbols such as parentheses or curly brackets, the matching bracket pair is automatically added in the JavaScript editor when the first pair is typed.
steps.instructions:
Use an array to store the 3 sprite images!


An array is an ordered list of elements with the same data type. Create an array in JavaScript that contains a list of image variables.


Underneath // array and variable set up, use the keyword let to declare a new array called spriteList. Type an assignment operator, then use a pair of brackets [ ] to contain the elements in the array. 


Inside the brackets [ ], type the names of the 3 sprite image variables declared under // sprite images separated by commas. The code might look like: 

let spriteList = [puppyImage, catImage, snakeImage]

Now, the 3 sprite images are stored in the spriteList array to be used in the project.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you replace the img`...` parameter of the sprites.create function with code that will pull an element from the spriteList array using the counter variable?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is the spriteList array and the loop’s counter variable used in the sprites.create code?

❓ How many times will the for loop run? What will happen on each iteration?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that a for loop has 3 expressions, separated by semicolons: initialization, run condition, and increment.

💡 Because the counter variable begins at 0 and will continue running while the count is less than 3, the for loop will run 3 times. Each time it runs, a new sprite will be created with an image selected from the spriteList array at the index that is equivalent to the counter variable.
steps.instructions:
Use a for loop to create a row of sprites from an array!


Open Loops and drag [for] underneath the existing code under // project code. 


Change the counter variable i to count in all 3 expressions, then update the run condition to count < 3 so the loop will run 3 times.


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] inside the curly brackets { } of the for loop. Replace the img`...` parameter with the name of the sprite array by typing spriteList and a pair of brackets [ ]. Type the count variable inside the brackets [ ] so the counter variable will pull all 3 images in the spriteList array to create 3 different sprites as the for loop runs.


Click ▶ to see the sprite images appear on the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the xOffset and spacing variables to spread out the 3 sprites across the middle of the screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How are the x-positions of each of the Player sprites calculated? 

❓ Where will each sprite appear on the screen? How do you know?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Each time the for loop runs, a new sprite will be created and its position will be set. First, the sprite’s width will be added with the value of the spacing variable (20). Then, the sum will be multiplied by the current value of the loop’s counter variable. After, the product will be added with the value of the xOffset variable (40) to set the sprite’s x-position.

💡 Each sprite will appear in a row at the same y-position (60) and will be placed 20 pixels apart.
steps.instructions:
Spread out the 3 sprites across the middle of the screen!


Create 2 new variables to offset and add spacing between each sprite and the left side of the screen. Under the array declarations under // array and variable set up, create a variable named xOffset, set to 40, and a variable named spacing, set to 20.


Under // project code, set the sprite’s x-position inside the curly brackets { } of the for loop. Inside a pair of parentheses, add the values of spacing and the width of the sprite. Multiply the total by the count counter variable. This will spread out the 3 sprites. Add the value of xOffset to the end of the equation to offset the row of sprites from the left side of the screen. The code may look like:


mySprite.x = count * (mySprite.width + spacing) + xOffset


Click ▶ to see 3 sprites spread out across the middle of the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you declare the type of the empty nameList array after the colon :?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why does the type need to be defined when creating an empty array? 

❓ What types of values can be stored in an array?

❓ What symbols need to be included when declaring an empty array?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that an array can be made up of images, string, number, or sprite values. However, all elements in the array must be of the same type. As a result, it’s important to define what type of elements the empty array will store, so that the program is unable to add different types of elements into the same array.

💡 Make sure the ninja has included a colon :, the type string, and a pair of brackets [ ] before the assignment operator in the nameList array declaration code. Point out to the ninja that the string type appears in blue, has a lowercase s, and is singular.
steps.instructions:
Create an empty array to store user provided strings!


Underneath // array and variable set up, use the keyword let to declare an array called nameList. When creating an array without any initial elements, its type must be declared by typing a colon, the type, and a pair of brackets [ ] after its name. Since nameList will contain strings, use : string [] after the array name. Then, type an assignment operator and a second pair of brackets [ ], so that the code looks like: 

let nameList: string[] = []

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add the push function to the array name, inside the for loop?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How many times will the for loop run? How do you know?

❓ What does the push function do? How might it be used in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that the for loop will run 3 times. The counter variable will begin at 1, then continue to run while the count is less than 4 and increase by 1 each time. The variable will count 1, 2, 3 instead of 0, 1, 2.

💡 In JavaScript, push is a function that adds an element to the end of an array. In the next step, the ninja will add code to add user-submitted strings to the end of an array.
steps.instructions:
Push elements to the empty array!


Underneath // project code, create a few new lines above the existing code. Open Loops and drag [for] underneath the comment. 


In the initialization expression, replace 0 with 1 to change where the counter variable begins, then update the run condition to i < 4 so the loop will run 3 times.


Inside the curly brackets { } of the for loop, type the name of the empty array and a dot operator . then select push from the code completion tool and type a pair of parentheses( ) so that the code looks like: nameList.push()


﻿The push function adds an element to the end of an array.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add a game.askForString function inside the parentheses of nameList.push()?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is the askForString function different from the askForNumber function?

❓ What will appear on the screen each time the for loop runs?

❓ What will happen to the user-submitted strings?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that the askForString function asks the user for a string value, whereas the askForNumber function asks the user for a number value. They both create an answer box on the screen and have message and answerLength parameters.

💡 Each time the for loop runs, a dialog box appears that asks the user to submit a string. The loop’s counter variable is used in the message so that the correct number appears on each iteration. The first time the message will say “Name Sprite #1”, then “Name Sprite #2, and finally “Name Sprite #3”.
steps.instructions:
Fill the empty array with 3 strings provided by the user!


Click Game, then drag [ask for string] inside the parentheses of nameList.push(). Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

game.askForString(null)

The askForString function takes 2 parameters: message and answerLength. Update the message parameter with a string that asks the user for 3 different sprite names, concatenated with the i counter variable to show the number of each name being asked for. Update the answerLength parameter to limit how long the user’s answer can be.


When the user enters a new name, the string will be pushed, or added, to the nameList array in the order that they are submitted, and can be used later in the project.


Click ▶ to fill the empty array with 3 sprite names!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you replace the string parameter in the sayText function with code that will pull an element from the nameList array depending on the counter variable’s index?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the sayText code know which value to pull from the nameList array?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja how nameList[count] is used in the text parameter of the sayText code. Each time a sprite appears on the screen, it pulls the value from the nameList array with an index that matches the current value of the loop’s counter variable. The first time the loop runs, the first element in the nameList array (0) will be used as the first sprite’s name. The counter variable and index will increase by 1 each time the for loop runs.
steps.instructions:
Have each sprite say their name!


Open Sprites and drag [(this) say (:))] underneath the Player sprite’s position code inside the for loop. Replace the string parameter with nameList and a pair of brackets [ ]. Inside the brackets [ ], type the counter variable count. 


As the counter variable increases, the loop will use the counter variable’s value to access a different string from the nameList array. Each Player sprite will say a string from the array, in the order they were submitted.


Click ▶ to see each sprite say their names!

steps.hints: ❓ What directions would help users understand how the game is played?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What background color might you use as a backdrop for the project?

❓ What directions might tell the user how to play the game? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja that they can always click on the palette for one of the images in the code to open the editor. Once opened, they can hover their cursor over each individual color to find the corresponding value to use as a background color.

💡 Remind the ninja that strings need to be placed inside of quotation marks and that parameters need to be separated by a comma, otherwise the code will not be able to run correctly.
steps.instructions:
Finish the project by adding a background color and directions to the beginning of the project!


Open Scene, drag [set background color to (color)] under // project code. Click between the parentheses to set a color parameter using a number 1-15.


Open Game and drag [show long text (str) (layout)] underneath the setBackgroundColor code. Update the string and layout parameters, so that the dialog box shares directions for the user to follow.


Click ▶ to see the directions and background color!

subgroups.title: What’s in a Name?
subgroups.introduction: Create a project that adds user-provided strings to an empty array.

validationItems.text: Create an array to contain 3 sprite image variables.
Use a for loop to create sprites from the images.
Use offset and spacing variables to position the three sprites.
Create an empty array to store strings.
Use a for loop to add elements to the empty string array.
Use the sprite and name arrays to have each sprite say its name.
Change the background color and add directions for the user.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 3 of Purple Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about arrays and several functions available to help you create and update arrays in JavaScript. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 3:

badges.title: Making a List, Checking it Twice
badges.description: Create and modify arrays within a program in JavaScript.

badges.title: Array of Sunshine
badges.description: Create an array in JavaScript.

badges.title: A Lengthy Calculation
badges.description: Calculate the length of an array.

badges.title: I Choose You!
badges.description: Access an element based on its index in an array.

badges.title: Objects May Be Larger Than They Appear
badges.description: Change the scale of a sprite.

badges.title: You’ll Fit Right In
badges.description: Use the push function to add an element to the end of an array.

badges.title: A String of Questions
badges.description: Use the askForString function to prompt the user for a string response.

badges.title: For Each Its Own
badges.description: Use a for element of loop to iterate through all the elements in an array.

badges.title: Search Engine
badges.description: Use the indexOf function to find the index of a provided value in an array.

badges.title: You’re Outta Here
badges.description: Use the removeAt function to remove a specific element from an array.
